intro.html:
Checkable list to improve security and privacy. The lists are sorted in sequential order with top priority first, so move through the list top-down. 

You can also download a personal copy for future use.

items.text: Install uBlock Origin in your main browser. Confirm the developer is Raymond Hill ("gorhill") before installing.
Set your default search engine to Brave or DuckDuckGo instead of Google or Bing.
Sign up for a password manager (ProtonPass or KeePassXC are good free starting points).
Change your email and banking passwords to unique, manager-generated ones first.
items.details: You can generate strong passwords for free here.

items.text: Turn on two-factor authentication with an authenticator app (not SMS) on your email account.
items.details: Some good options are: ente and Aegis Authenticator, or you can explore some more here.

items.text: Turn off your phone’s advertising ID.
items.details:
• Android: Settings, search "advertising ID," delete it.
  • iOS: Settings, Privacy & Security, Tracking, turn off "Allow Apps to Request to Track."

items.text: Check your email address at haveibeenpwned.com to see if it’s already been exposed in a breach.
Stop using "Log in with Google/Facebook" on other websites going forward; use your password manager instead.
Turn on 2FA with an authenticator app on your password manager, bank, and any other account you’d consider catastrophic to lose.
Install Signal and move at least one sensitive conversation to it.
Set up email aliasing (Firefox Relay or DuckDuckGo Email Protection) and use a new alias the next time a site asks for your email.
Opt out of the highest-priority data brokers using the Big Ass Data Broker Opt-Out List (BADBOOL); start with its top tier of roughly 14 sites.
Freeze your credit for free with Experian, Equifax, TransUnion, Innovis, and ChexSystems.
Turn off Google Location History, or set it to auto-delete every few months, at myaccount.google.com/activitycontrols/location.
Review your phone’s app permissions for location, camera, microphone, and contacts, and turn off anything you don’t actively need.
Set Firefox or LibreWolf’s Enhanced Tracking Protection to Strict (or confirm Brave’s Shields are on, which they are by default).
Turn on DNS over HTTPS in your browser’s network settings.
Decline notification permission requests from websites by default.

blocks.title: A Little More Work, but Still Easy

items.text: Get a hardware security key (like a YubiKey) for your email and password manager if you’re ready for the strongest available 2FA tier.
Scrub metadata from photos before sharing anything sensitive (use your phone’s built-in "remove location" share option, or a tool like ExifCleaner).
Sign up for an encrypted cloud storage provider (Proton Drive, Sync.com) or wrap your existing cloud storage with Cryptomator.
Set up a real local backup (external drive or NAS), and actually test restoring a file from it once.
Get a secondary phone number (TextNow, Hushed, or MySudo) for lower-stakes sign-ups, so your real number isn’t everywhere.
Check your mobile carrier’s privacy dashboard and opt out of ad targeting and data sharing.
Run coveryourtracks.eff.org and globalprivacycontrol.org to confirm your browser protections are actually working.
Set up your IRS Identity Protection PIN at irs.gov and check your Social Security account at ssa.gov.
Consider a VPN from a provider with a verified no-logs track record (Mullvad or IVPN, for example) if hiding your activity from your ISP matters to you.

blocks.title: More Complex, Might Not Be Needed for Everyone

items.text: Re-run coveryourtracks.eff.org and globalprivacycontrol.org after any browser or OS update.
Check haveibeenpwned.com every few months for new breach exposures.
Revisit your BADBOOL opt-outs yearly — data brokers tend to repopulate listings over time.
Review app and browser extension permissions quarterly, and remove anything you no longer use.
Rotate the password for any account involved in a new breach immediately.
Keep your password manager, OS, and browser updated to the latest version.
Clean your phone of sensitive content.
Remove social media apps you don’t need.
Delete messages related to the protest.
Remove contact names for fellow protesters (use nicknames).
Use a long passcode (6+ characters with letters and numbers).
Turn OFF Face ID (iPhone) / fingerprint unlock (Android).
Turn off location services.
Turn off Bluetooth.
Turn off WiFi when not needed.
Consider a secondary "sanitized" phone.
Wear a mask (health + facial recognition evasion).
Don’t drive your own car (license plate scanners).
Don’t go alone — go with a group.
If using a burner/secondary phone, use a separate phone number (eSIM works).
Don’t connect the burner phone to WiFi at home, and never power it on at home.
Never have both phones powered on at the same location.
Don’t save WiFi networks on the burner phone; use a long passcode with no biometrics.
At the event, keep your phone in airplane mode if possible.
Use encrypted messaging (Signal, not SMS).
Don’t post real-time location updates.
Be aware of surveillance cameras.
Recognize flock cameras (license plate readers).
Know your rights (you can refuse to unlock your phone).
Travel with a "sanitized" phone for your trip.
Use separate communication accounts on your travel phone.
Consider wiping the phone before travel and restoring after.
